To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) low coordination, random, distributed node wakeup policies are effective in generating connected-covered topologies in dense deployments, and (ii) simple distributed algorithms can be designed that realize these policies with low message exchange overhead.

(1) in dense sensor deployments, the use of random wakeup policies can construct near optimal topologies, (2) the use of wakeup policies that follow a specific pattern can construct topologies that have similar properties as the optimal topologies and (3) these policies are easy to implement and require zero coordination between nodes.

(1) in dense sensor networks, the construction of near-optimal topological cover can be achieved with zero coordination between sensor nodes, and (2) distributed algorithms can be designed to construct near-optimal sensor network topologies with low message-exchange and computation overheads.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of how nodes should self-organize to form a connected-covered network in the presence of node failures.
the question of how to manage sensor nodes in dense sensor deployments so as to increase the lifetime of sensor networks, while maintaining the desired coverage and connectivity requirements.
developing low-coordination topology construction policies that can efficiently construct connected-covered sensor topologies, and hence improve the fault-tolerance of the sensor network.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in dense sensor deployments, low-coordination wakeup policies for sensor networks can be used to efficiently construct near-optimal, connected-covered topologies with low message overhead, as long as sensor location information is available.

in dense deployments, the proposed low-coordination, distributed wakeup policies and algorithms are able to efficiently construct connected-covered topological structures, and hence provide good fault tolerance to the network.

the proposed wakeup based topology construction policies and algorithms can be used to construct multiple, independent, near-optimal sensor network topologies, with zero or minimal coordination, in dense deployments, with very little message exchange overhead.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide a framework for constructing connected-covered topologies with low coordination and low message overhead, and show that this framework is effective for dense deployments.

we propose and evaluate distributed, low-coordinated, wakeup policies for sensor networks to construct near-optimal connected-coverage topologies with zero coordination between sensors and also propose distributed topology construction algorithms that achieve the same performance bounds in realistic deployment scenarios with varying node densities and limited location information.
we propose and study a few simple distributed algorithms that can construct near-optimum topologies in dense sensor networks, with zero or very low message exchange overhead.
The main takeaway from our work is that

in dense deployments, it is possible to construct near-optimal connected-covered topologies with zero or very low levels of coordination between sensor nodes, which is a very desirable feature for large-scale deployments.

the network can be made highly fault tolerant with a small increase in the number of active sensor nodes, and this increase in the number is small compared to that required for fault tolerance in traditional sensor networks.
the use of multiple, low-coordination topologies can provide good fault tolerance in dense sensor deployments with low message-exchange and energy consumption overhead.
